problems.description: GET /health is served through the websockets HTTP handshake hook rather than a real HTTP layer. Sessions 2-4 of this story add /channels and /channels/{name}/subscribers REST endpoints, which this approach cannot cleanly serve, so session 2 will need to rework the REST surface.

Inconsistent validation exceptions: make_message raises ValueError while parse_client_message raises MessageError for the same class of protocol violation; server.py's _dispatch catches only MessageError, so a ValueError raised via make_message path would escape the handler.
Direct messages do not validate target_id presence before routing; a 'direct' message without target_id produces an 'unknown target_id: None' error to the sender instead of a clear protocol error.

Discrepancy flag: the listed convention violations for __init__.py ('Classes should use PascalCase', 'Functions should use snake_case') reference empty files containing no such symbols and appear to be linter false positives; the visible substantive code (messages.py, registry.py, server.py) follows snake_case functions and PascalCase classes consistently.
registry.all() returns a dict copy on every broadcast so messages can be sent concurrently; acceptable at current scale but the copy-per-message cost grows linearly with fan-out in later sessions.

strengths: Clean module decomposition (messages/registry/server/storage) that maps directly onto the 5-session story arc, separating protocol, connection state, and persistence concerns.
Message envelope matches the story spec exactly: {type, payload, timestamp} with broadcast/direct/system types and validation on parse.
Thread-safe ClientRegistry with a lock, and _safe_send guards against ConnectionClosed during fan-out, so a single dead client cannot break a broadcast.
Public signatures carry type hints and follow snake_case/PascalCase naming per project conventions.
Measured zero new bugs, zero duplication, and a compact event-based design that makes later Redis/SQLite sessions a natural extension.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, spec-conformant greenfield session with a sensible module split and honest measurements (no bugs, no duplication), though the websockets-handshake-hook REST surface is a minor forward-looking liability for later sessions.

problems.description: _handle_subscribe and _handle_unsubscribe duplicate the channel-validation + error/ack pattern; a shared helper (and the resulting conditional branches) are largely responsible for the +16 cognitive complexity and 6 smells.

The only test change in the visible diff updates the SUPPORTED_TYPES constant; no tests are shown covering ChannelRegistry, the subscribe/unsubscribe handlers, channel-scoped broadcast, or the new /channels REST endpoints (new test files may exist outside the truncated diff).

Channel-scoped broadcast routes by filtering the full client registry against the subscriber set on every send, coupling message delivery to subscription lookups; acceptable at this scale, but a per-channel fan-out map would be cleaner as channels grow.
Channel names are unvalidated client input (no length/character limits) and the REST path regex does not URL-decode the channel segment before lookup.

strengths: ChannelRegistry mirrors the existing lock-based ClientRegistry pattern in registry.py, a strong convention match.
Clean lifecycle handling: unsubscribe_all is invoked on disconnect, preventing stale channel membership.
The _json_response helper refactor removes duplication across the REST handlers.
New message types and REST endpoints follow the established dispatch and section-comment conventions.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-fitted feature addition that mirrors existing registry and dispatch patterns, with only minor handler duplication and a test-coverage gap; the measured 0.75 convention score and listed violations largely reference untouched files (app.py, storage.py, __init__.py), so they are pre-existing rather than introduced by this commit.

problems.description: The service now maintains three overlapping persistence mechanisms for message state — the flat JSON-Lines audit trail, the new SQLite history store, and the Redis presence hash — with no clear ownership boundary, risking drift and redundant writes.

The module docstring previously stated 'no database is used anywhere in this service'; this commit silently flips that design contract, and the old JSONL audit trail is retained alongside SQLite rather than being consolidated.

MessageStore opens a fresh SQLite connection on every save_message/list_messages/clear call instead of reusing a connection, which is wasteful under load and reflects the +38 cognitive-complexity and +4 smells reported by SonarQube.
list_messages uses LIMIT/OFFSET pagination against an unbounded messages table with no index on channel/timestamp and no retention policy, so history grows without bound and deep pagination degrades.

The measured convention score of 0.75 is dragged down by violations in files outside this diff (app.py, __init__.py, registry.py, storage.py); the new db.py and redis_backend.py code itself follows snake_case/PascalCase/UPPER_CASE conventions correctly, so the score over-penalizes this commit.
clear() issues an unconditional DELETE with no guardrails, making accidental production data loss trivial if ever wired to an exposed endpoint.

strengths: Clean module separation: db.py (SQLite history), redis_backend.py (pub/sub + presence), server.py (integration) each have a single focused responsibility.
All SQL uses parameterized queries, so there is no injection surface in the new persistence code.
Graceful environment-driven configuration: falls back to fakeredis when REDIS_URL is unset, keeping standalone dev and tests working (matching the project's operational conventions).
The presence hash in Redis is a sound design — client-to-server mapping survives any single server restart and is visible across instances.
The listen() loop defensively skips non-message pub/sub frames and silently drops malformed payloads instead of crashing the worker.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent multi-instance integration (Redis pub/sub backbone + SQLite history) with clean module boundaries and injection-safe SQL, but it silently overturns the documented 'no database' design, stacks a third persistence layer on top of the JSONL audit trail, and accrues moderate maintainability/performance debt.

problems.description: In the shown variant the transport owns the client registry (`self.registry = self.transport.registry`), coupling client_id-to-connection bookkeeping into the transport layer. The BaseTransport docstring correctly claims connections are opaque to the core, but this wiring leaks registry semantics through the seam; the server (not the transport) should own the registry and hand connections back through send/broadcast.

The new transport seam (BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport, TRANSPORTS selection) has no dedicated unit tests — the added tests cover broker, store, and redis, but nothing exercises a fake transport to prove the routing core stays transport-agnostic.
Module-level constants in __init__.py, registry.py, and storage.py remain non-UPPER_CASE (part of the 30 violations / 0.75 score), though these are pre-existing files this commit did not modify.

Cognitive complexity increased by +7 from splitting the handler into _on_client_connect/_on_client_disconnect/_on_client_message; acceptable for the abstraction split, but the dispatch method still holds several branches.

strengths: Clean dependency inversion: the routing core depends only on the BaseTransport ABC and never imports a network library, making SSE/long-polling additions a single-file change.
Consistent dependency injection across the constructor (broker, presence, store, rate_limiter, transport), matching the existing module layout and helper patterns.
TRANSPORT env var plus the TRANSPORTS registry in server.py is a simple, discoverable extension point with a clear error on unknown names.
Measured quality delta is clean: bugs +0, smells +0, duplications -0.2% — the refactor removes more than it adds.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-grounded strategy-pattern refactor that cleanly decouples routing from WebSocket I/O with injectable dependencies and a pluggable transport registry; the 0.75 convention score reflects mostly pre-existing debt in untouched files, while the only real gap is a lack of direct tests for the new transport seam.

problems.description: RateLimiter reaches through self.redis.client, coupling to the raw redis client instead of going through the RedisBackend abstraction the rest of the server uses (presence mirroring, etc.). Bypasses the established seam.

Single session's diff adds +34 cognitive complexity and +13 smells; background cleanup task plus rate-limiting wiring are concentrated in server.py's constructor/lifecycle and could be extracted into dedicated components.
resolve_message_ttl_days() returns a float for a day count that is semantically an integer, causing type drift between the config resolver and its use in cutoff_iso(timedelta).

Measured convention score 0.75 is dragged down by pre-existing violations in files this commit does not touch (app.py, __init__.py, registry.py, storage.py PascalCase/snake_case/UPPER_CASE); the new code itself (rate_limit.py, db.py additions) follows PascalCase classes, snake_case functions, and UPPER_CASE constants correctly. Flagging this discrepancy between the codebase-wide score and the commit's own output.

Fixed-window counter only sets EXPIRE when INCR returns 1; if expire fails (or the key pre-exists without TTL), the counter persists and the client is permanently rate-limited rather than getting a fresh window.

strengths: resolve_rate_limit()/resolve_message_ttl_days() mirror the existing resolve_database_path() env-resolution pattern exactly
Rate limiting lives in its own module (rate_limit.py) with UPPER_CASE constants, cleanly separated from transport concerns
Redis-based counters correctly share the limit across server instances, matching the existing presence-mirroring design
Pagination with has_more flag is well-formed and backed by a matching (channel, timestamp) index added to the schema
Over-limit clients receive an explicit 'system'/'error' reply rather than a silent drop
Background TTL purge is configurable via env, consistent with the codebase's resolve_* convention
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, pattern-consistent feature session (rate limiting, paginated history, TTL cleanup) that fits the existing architecture well but adds meaningful cognitive complexity and slightly bypasses the RedisBackend abstraction seam.

compounding_issues: threading.RLock guards the client registry inside a single-threaded asyncio event loop (introduced S1, persisted through S5) — unnecessary and signals concurrency-model confusion, though harmless at this scale.
Dual inverse maps (channels -> _client_channels) must be updated symmetrically in _set_subscription, the disconnect path, and Redis bookkeeping (S2/S3), creating drift risk as feature surface grew.

Redis coupling in S3: when Redis is present, even local delivery routes through pub/sub (self-listener), so a mid-run Redis outage silently breaks broadcast; the graceful-degradation fallback only covers the no-Redis-at-startup case.

Hand-rolled asyncio HTTP parsing (S1) persisted across all sessions, so every added endpoint (/messages, /channels, /history) required manual query-string/route parsing and error handling rather than a framework.
key_decisions: S1 replaced the Flask seed with a dependency-light asyncio + websockets implementation and a hand-rolled HTTP server, committing to that stack for all five sessions.
S2 added a channel subscription model with dual bookkeeping maps and a wire format supporting channel in top-level or payload.
S3 integrated Redis pub/sub and SQLite persistence as an optional, env-configured operational backbone with graceful degradation when Redis is absent.
S4 extracted a pluggable transport seam (BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport) into transport.py, decoupling connection lifecycle from notification routing and keeping all tests green.

S5 layered cross-cutting concerns onto existing seams: Redis-backed per-client rate limiting with local fallback, message TTL cleanup loop, and a paginated /history endpoint reading the S3 messages table.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality arcs steadily upward. S1 delivers a clean, well-separated greenfield server (architectural fit 0.75, zero new bugs), S2 cleanly adds channels with regression tests (0.88, no debt), S3 makes the largest feature jump with Redis/SQLite integration that introduces moderate complexity and coupling, S4 is a disciplined pure refactor that pays down structure without regressing any of the 8 tests, and S5 finishes with thoughtful cross-cutting work — rate limiting, TTL cleanup, history — that directly reuses the S3 persistence and S4 transport seams. Test coverage grew monotonically 4->6->8->8->10, all passing at the final state.
story_review.summary: A textbook multi-session arc (greenfield -> feature -> integration -> refactor -> cross-cutting) where every later session builds on prior seams, quality improves monotonically, and final tests all pass.
